turns.text: Kicking off structural calcs for HOS-2417, Alder Street Commons in Tacoma. Eight stories: Level 1 retail podium with a steel transfer level at L2 on concrete spread footings, Levels 3-8 glulam post-and-beam with CLT floor panels, Type IV-B construction, roof at L8. Lateral system is steel buckling-restrained braced frames (BRBF) in the two stair/elevator cores. Design basis I'm carrying for the superstructure: 2021 IBC with Washington amendments, ASCE 7-16, NDS 2018, AISC 360-16 and AISC 341-16. Ridgeline Geotechnical's preliminary report says Site Class C. Ground snow 25 psf, Risk Category II. Seismic weight from the Revit takeoff is W = 8,640 kips, h_n = 92 ft. For ASCE 7-16 Site Class C the hazard tool gives SDS = 0.91 g and SD1 = 0.50 g. Can you set up the equivalent lateral force base shear for the BRBF (R = 8, Omega_o = 2.5, Cd = 5)?

Equivalent lateral force, ASCE 7-16 Section 12.8. Approximate period: Ta = Ct * h_n^x = 0.03 * 92^0.75 = 0.89 s (BRBF uses Ct = 0.03, x = 0.75 per Table 12.8-2). Cs = SDS/(R/Ie) = 0.91/(8/1.0) = 0.114, but it need not exceed SD1/(T*(R/Ie)) = 0.50/(0.89 * 8) = 0.0702. Minimum Cs = 0.044*SDS*Ie = 0.040 (and S1 < 0.6 g so Eq. 12.8-6 does not apply). Governing Cs = 0.0702. Base shear V = Cs*W = 0.0702 * 8,640 kips = 607 kips. Vertical distribution exponent k = 1.0 + (0.89 - 0.5)/2 = 1.20. Design story drift limit for Risk Category II, structure over 4 stories: Delta_a = 0.020 h_sx. Note: if you later get a computed period from the ETABS model you may use Cu*Ta = 1.4*0.89 = 1.25 s as the cap for strength, which would reduce Cs further, but I'd keep 0.89 s until the model is calibrated.

turns.text: Good. Gravity framing assumptions for the typical residential floors L3-L8: CLT floor panels 5-ply 175 mm grade V2 spanning about 19 ft between glulam beams, 3 in normalweight concrete topping over an acoustic mat, superimposed dead 15 psf, partitions 15 psf, residential live 40 psf, corridors 100 psf. Glulam is 24F-V8 DF/DF for beams and girders, 24F-1.8E? no, columns are Combination 2 DF. Can you sanity-check the floor self-weight?

Self-weight check: 5-ply 175 mm (6.89 in) V2 CLT at roughly 31 pcf = 6.89/12 * 31 = 17.8 psf. 3 in normalweight topping at 150 pcf = 37.5 psf. Acoustic mat about 1 psf. Glulam beams/girders smeared at about 5 psf. Total structural dead load is about 61 psf, plus 15 psf superimposed and 15 psf partitions = 91 psf for gravity design (partition load is live per ASCE 7 Section 4.3.2 but include at least 10 psf in seismic weight per 12.7.2). That is consistent with your 8,640 kips seismic weight if the floor plate is around 16,500 sf. One caution: 175 mm V2 at a 19 ft span will be governed by vibration rather than bending; I'd flag that before the peer reviewer does.

turns.text: One more: what's the redundancy factor situation for the BRBF cores? Two frames per direction per core, so four per direction total.

With two cores and two BRB frames per direction in each core (four per direction), removal of any one brace typically won't cause more than a 33% reduction in story strength and won't create an extreme torsional irregularity, so you can usually justify rho = 1.0 under ASCE 7-16 Section 12.3.4.2 condition (a), provided the cores are reasonably balanced in plan. If the north core frames carry noticeably more than half the story shear in the ETABS run, check the brace-removal case explicitly; otherwise use rho = 1.3 conservatively for the collectors and frames. turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Fire design question. Type IV-B needs a 2-hour rating on the primary frame (columns, girders) and on floor construction. Exposed glulam will be designed by the NDS Chapter 16 calculated method. Nominal char rate beta_n = 1.5 in/hr. What effective char depth do I take for 2 hours, and what's the formula?

NDS 2018 Section 16.2.1: beta_t = beta_n / t^0.187 where t is in hours but the nominal rate is defined at 1 hr, so beta_t = 1.5 in/hr. Char depth a_char = beta_t * t^0.813 = 1.5 * 2^0.813 = 2.64 in (67 mm). Effective char depth a_eff = 1.2 * a_char = 3.2 in (81 mm) for a 2-hour exposure, which matches NDS Table 16.2.1A. For reference, the same table gives 1.8 in (46 mm) for 1 hour and 2.5 in (64 mm) for 1.5 hours. Apply a_eff to every exposed face, then check the residual section with the NDS Table 16.2.2 design stress to member strength factors (2.85 for bending and tension, 2.58 for compression parallel to grain, 2.03 for beam and column buckling). Don't forget the outer lam rule: for glulam bending members designed for fire, replace one core lam with one tension lam per NDS 16.2.4.

S_r = 2.35*20.8^2/6 = 169 in^3 (2,770 cm^3). Fire load combination is D + L (no load factors for the ASD fire check) with M = 117 kip-ft (159 kN-m): fb = 117*12/169 = 8.31 ksi (57.3 MPa). The 8-3/4 width is too narrow for a 2-hour three-sided exposure; you'll need 10-3/4 or encapsulation (two layers of 5/8 Type X on the girder sides would get you there per 2021 IBC 722.7 but Marcus wants it exposed).

(3) Wind: minor changes; ground elevation factor Ke and tornado loads don't apply to Risk Category II. (4) Collector and diaphragm design: Section 12.10.3 alternative diaphragm design provisions may be attractive for the CLT diaphragm. (5) Drift and stability: no major change for BRBF. turns.text: For PR-09: 5-ply 175 mm V2, span 19 ft simply supported, topping 3 in NW, my target is f1 of at least 8.0 Hz. What does it come out to?

Using f1 = (pi/(2*L^2)) * sqrt(EI_eff/m), with EI_eff for 175 mm V2 about 440e6 lbf-in^2/ft (Cascadia's published value) and mass including the 3 in topping and 15 psf SDL: f1 = 7.6 Hz for the 175 mm V2 panels, below your 8.0 Hz target. Options: (a) 5-ply 191 mm E1, EI_eff about 640e6 lbf-in^2/ft, gives f1 = 9.1 Hz; (b) 7-ply 245 mm V2 gives about 11.3 Hz but adds 4.3 psf and 2 in of depth; (c) add a mid-span glulam beam, which Marcus will hate. I recommend option (a): 5-ply 191 mm E1 at 9.1 Hz meets the target with 0.63 in (16 mm) more depth than the 175 mm. Also confirm with the CLT Handbook span criterion L_lim = 0.11*(EI_eff)^0.29/m^0.12 as a cross-check; for the E1 191 mm it gives about 20.4 ft, above the 19 ft span.

turns.text: Go with 5-ply 191 mm E1 for all typical floor panels L3-L8. Roof stays 5-ply 175 mm V2 since there's no topping and no occupancy vibration concern. I'll update the spec section 06 17 19 and tell Cascadia. Now PR-21: what screw recommendation should I put on the diaphragm detail?

Observation (not a nonconformance): construction debris and loose screws on the Level 6 CLT deck adjacent to panel joints; recommend housekeeping before spline installation to avoid screws being driven through debris. Recommend contractor provide weather protection for exposed CLT panel edges. No EOR disposition required.

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Is FO-7 something I need to respond to? And is the water staining at L5 a structural concern?

FO-7 is a field observation, not a nonconformance, and explicitly states no EOR disposition is required; a brief acknowledgment to Northgate is enough. On the L5 staining: surface staining from a single rain event is typically cosmetic, but CLT that stays wet can develop checking and dimensional change as it dries, and wetted edges at panel joints can affect the spline screw embedment. Ask Pellham for: (1) a written moisture management plan per the mass timber spec; (2) confirmation that the stained panels will be allowed to dry before topping; (3) photos of the joint edges. If any panels show standing water at joints, require drying before the spline screws go in. I would not issue an NCR on staining alone.

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Then the RTU thing. Four RTUs at 4,850 lb each on a steel dunnage frame, bearing on the L8 roof glulam beams at four points per unit. The roof is 5-ply 175 mm V2 with no topping. Quick check whether the roof beams under it (6-3/4 x 19-1/2 24F-V8 at 22 ft span) can take it.

Per RTU: 4,850 lb (21.6 kN) over four dunnage points = 1,213 lb (5.4 kN) per point; assume two points land on each beam at roughly the third points. Added moment per beam = 1.21*22/3 = 8.9 kip-ft (12.1 kN-m). Existing roof beam D + S moment (with S = 22.4 psf at 10 ft tributary): about 31 kip-ft (42 kN-m). Total 39.9 kip-ft. 6-3/4 x 19-1/2: S = 428 in^3, fb = 39.9*12/428 = 1.12 ksi (7.7 MPa) vs F'b = 2.40*1.0 (CD for snow 1.15 -> 2.76 ksi) * CV 0.96 = 2.65 ksi. DCR = 0.42. OK. Check the dunnage support detail for local bearing on the beam top (perpendicular-to-grain, Fc_perp = 650 psi): a 4 in x 6 in bearing plate gives 1,213/24 = 51 psi, fine. Also confirm the mechanical engineer's operating weight; 4,850 lb sounds like shipping weight and operating may be higher.

Description: Longitudinal split/check approximately 3/8 in wide at the surface and 30 in long, starting 14 in below the beam seat, depth by feeler gauge 2-1/4 in. Exceeds the visual acceptance limit in the ANSI A190.1 appearance and grading criteria referenced in the specification. Reference: specification 06 18 00. Disposition requested from EOR. Status: OPEN.

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: NCR-3: Column C-4 at L4 has a 3/8 in wide by 30 in long split, 2-1/4 in deep, just below the beam seat. Axial load at that level is about 118 kips D+L. What do you suggest?

Assessment: a 2-1/4 in (57 mm) deep split in a 10-3/4 in wide column below a beam seat mainly reduces shear and bearing capacity locally and can propagate under seasonal drying. Axial capacity of 10-3/4 x 10-1/2 Comb. 2 DF at L4 with 118 kips (525 kN) demand: P'c is about 195 kips, DCR 0.61, and a single split of this depth doesn't change the axial capacity significantly. But the seat connection relies on the screws within 18 in of the beam seat. Suggested disposition: reinforce with two rows of four 8 mm x 300 mm fully threaded self-tapping screws installed perpendicular to the split, at 3 in (76 mm) spacing, starting 4 in above the split end, and fill the check with a structural epoxy only if Studio Fenwick wants it cosmetically. Northgate to measure the split width again in 60 days; if it grows beyond 1/2 in, replace the column segment. I'd keep the column in place.

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Agreed, use that. Send it as the disposition.

turns.text: Subject: C-4 column at L4. Dana, re NCR-3, Studio Fenwick prefers the check be left visible but cleaned rather than epoxy-filled; it's in a unit closet and will be behind gypsum on one side anyway. Please confirm the screws can be countersunk and plugged with face-grain DF plugs. Marcus

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Marcus wants the C-4 reinforcing screws countersunk and plugged, no epoxy. Any issue?

No structural issue. Countersinking the 8 mm x 300 mm fully threaded screws by up to 3/8 in (10 mm) and plugging with face-grain DF plugs is fine as long as the threaded length on each side of the split stays at least 4 in (100 mm); with a 300 mm screw in a 10-3/4 in (273 mm) column, installed at a slight angle, that is satisfied. Do not glue the plugs with anything that could hide future split growth; Northgate's 60-day measurement should be taken on the open check, not at the plugs.

turns.speaker: Dana Okafor
turns.text: Also, Sam asked why we didn't need to reduce the BRB cores after the topping change dropped the base shear. Remind me what you told me then.

When the topping change dropped V from 752 kips (3,345 kN) to 713 kips (3,172 kN), I advised not to downsize the BRB cores: BRB-3 was at 7.25 in^2 (4,680 mm^2), its DCR only fell to about 0.87, and the capacity design of the L2 transfer girders, gussets and columns had already been completed with the 7.25 in^2 adjusted brace strength. Downsizing would have required redoing the capacity design and re-issuing the BRB shop drawings (S-044A was already approved) for little benefit. The extra margin also covers the accidental torsion and any future ETABS model refinement.
